https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgqd.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Police say their officers have secured "the crime scene" By Gabriela Pomeroy Published 27 August 2026 Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said. Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used. It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school. One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported. The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported. Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide". "The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger. "I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said. State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence". The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday. Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come. "We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said. A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added. Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany. https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/11/mag.text: Menü Kereső Decemberig havi 5 ezer forinttal támogatja a kormány a dízelautósok tankolását Gazdaság frissítve Kovács Pál Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Csaknem egymillió autótulajdonos kap havi 5000 forint támogatást decemberig az államtól, az intézkedés a maximum 150 lóerős, dízelmeghajtású kocsik tulajdonosaira vonatkozik – jelentette be Magyar Péter a Facebookon . A héten tovább emelkedtek az üzemanyagárak, a dízel ára négy éve nem volt ilyen magas . Magyar azt is bejelentette, hogy a mezőgazdasági felhasználók visszaigényelhetik a jövedéki adójuk bizonyos részét. A megemelkedett világpiaci árak miatt a korábbi védett ár és a piaci ár közötti különbözet körülbelül 5000 forint egy tankolásnál. Ezt a különbözetet havi egy alkalommal megtéríti a kormány, mondta a miniszterelnök. Az autósok decemberig összesen 20 ezer forint kompenzációban részesülnek. A támogatás vonatkozik az őstermelőkre és az egyéni vállalkozókra is, ha a nevükön van a gépkocsi. Magyar Péter szerint ez az intézkedés azokat hivatott támogatni, akiket a leginkább sújt a dízel árának növekedése. A miniszterelnök szerint egy családnál havi egy tankolás a jellemző, ezért decemberig egy hónapban egy tankolásra jár a juttatás. „Nem célunk és nem is feladatunk a nagy teljesítményű, drága gépjárművek tankolásához hozzájárulni a magyar adófizetők pénzén” – tette hozzá. „Az érintetteknek ehhez nem kell kérelmet benyújtaniuk. A NAV gépjárműadó kivetéséhez használt adatbázisa alapján a Magyar Államkincstár automatikusan arra a bankszámlára utalja a támogatást, amelyről a tulajdonos a gépjárműadót befizette. Ha ilyen számla nem áll rendelkezése, akkor a NAV-nál ismert másik bankszámlaszámra érkezik az összeg” – mondta Magyar Péter. A mezőgazdaságot érintően is tett bejelentést Magyar. Azt mondta, a mezőgazdasági felhasználók az idei év végéig a gázolaj árába épített jövedéki adó teljes összegét visszaigényelhetik. „Ezzel azt akarjuk elérni, hogy a világpiaci olajár-emelkedés minél kisebb mértékben épüljön be a magyar mezőgazdasági termelés költségeibe, majd onnan az élelmiszerárakba” – mondta. A kormányfő arról is említést tett, hogy az elmúlt hónapokban jelentősen megváltozott a világpiaci helyzet. Azt mondta, az áremelkedés ellenére még mindig nálunk szinte a legalacsonyabb a gázolaj átlagára Európában. Egyedül a tengerparttal rendelkező Horvátországban olcsóbb a dízel, de várhatóan ott is csak hétfőig, mondta. Magyar azt mondta, a jelenlegi árak mellett a védett ár bevezetése havonta mintegy 50–100 milliárd forintjába kerülne a költségvetésnek. A kormány most úgy döntött, hogy célzottan és fenntartható módon segítene, úgy, hogy az ne okozzon ellátási problémákat, mondta a miniszterelnök. A Fidesz egyébként a védett ár bevezetését kérte a parlament hétfői ülésén. Bóka János, a Fidesz frakcióvezetője azt mondta : a benzin átlagára nálunk 617 forint, a dízelé pedig 697 forint, miközben a védett ár 595 forint volt. Szerdán kormányülést tartottak, ahová Hernádi Zsoltot, a Mol elnök-vezérigazgatóját és a vállalat többi vezetőjét is behívatták . „Velük is tárgyalunk arról, hogyan és miként lehetne megfékezni ezt az elképesztő drágulást, már amennyire kivonhatja egy ország magát a világpiaci trendekből” – fogalmazott akkor Magyar Péter. A héten már sejthető volt, hogy célzott, és nem mindenkinek automatikusan járó támogatással tervez előállni a kormány. Erről a G7 cikkében olvashatnak részletesen . https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/03/latv.text: Polls opened on Saturday in Latvia's parliamentary election shaped by concerns over neighbouring Russia and a cost of living crisis.Some 1.5 million people are eligible to cast ballots in the parliamentary election, Latvia's 11th since gaining independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.The poll will see 14 parties run for 100 seats in the Saeima using a proportional system.Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.The Baltic state is a key pillar of NATO's eastern defensive flank, and experts say there is widespread support for Ukraine in the war with Russia."The stance towards Russia is the main reason for Latvians' Western, NATO and European anchoring," a Western diplomat in Riga said, adding that it would be hard to imagine major political changes.Polls predict the centre-right United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, will emerge the largest party in parliament in Saturday's vote.But his centre-right coalition, which also brings together the centrist New Unity, nationalist National Alliance and the Union of Greens and Farmers, is expected to emerge weakened from the election.The current governing coalition is made up of United List, New Unity, the Union of Greens and Farmers, and the National Alliance. Polls suggest the bloc is unlikely to retain power in its current form after the vote.Security and economy at the top of voters' mindsSecurity is at the top of voters' minds in a country bordering Russia which was annexed and ruled by Moscow for much of the 20th century.According to Roberts Kits, an analyst at the Latvian think tank LaSER, "defence and security will be the priority". Apart from a few dissenting voices, he said, there is broad consensus on maintaining military spending at nearly five percent of GDP and on supporting Ukraine.But the economy is also a major concern for voters.Latvia is the least affluent of the three Baltic States in terms of living standards, despite catching up since joining the EU in 2004.Growth is sluggish, with voters pointing to the cost of living, the state of the healthcare system and the difficulties of public finances. Complicating this are major regional disparities.The gap between Latvia's capital and the rest of the country is stark. Around Riga, GDP per capita reached 101 percent of the European average in 2024, according to a European Commission report. In other regions, the figure does not exceed 50 percent.The contrast is sharpest in Latgale, Latvia's easternmost region, where depopulation is accelerating and economic opportunity is scarce. The region is home to a large majority of Russian speakers, and its decline is reflected most visibly in Daugavpils, the country's second-largest city, where 90 percent of the population is Russian-speaking."The most important thing is the lack of young people and the lack of good jobs," said Aigars Soikants, a 30-year-old Daugavpils resident. "There isn't enough work. People are leaving."Despite living in a city with a predominantly Russian-speaking population, Soikants says identity is not what will drive his vote. He plans to back "a centrist or right-wing party which acts in the interest of the country."Rise of populist parties in LatviaSimilar to other parts of Europe, populist parties have benefited from economic worries in the lead-up to the election. The Sovereign Power (Suverena vara, SV) party, critical of aid to Ukraine and increasing military spending, is polling at nine percent and could reach second place in Parliament.Considered pro-Russian by its critics, the party, led by Julija Stepanenko, emphasises Latvia's economic difficulties. The party, however, is isolated politically and, barring a huge upset, has no chance of entering a future governing coalition.Carefully avoiding the word "Ukraine", Vjaceslavs Stepanenko, the head of SV's local list in Latgale and husband of the party’s chairwoman, advocates "stopping all aid to any foreign state"."We are the ones who need help, not the other way around."Another populist party, Latvia First (LPV), is also at nine percent, and its businessman leader Ainars Slesers is regularly compared to US President Donald Trump.The party is winning support with a conservative message and promises of economic revival, and unlike SV, it could become an indispensable partner in coalition talks."The big question is whether the United List will cooperate with Slesers' party," said political analyst Sigita Struberga.Can Russian-speaking voters influence the polls?Long rallied behind the "Harmony" party, Russian speakers, who make up about 35 percent of Latvia's population, no longer vote as a unified bloc.Harmony, which won several parliamentary elections without ever entering government, disappeared from parliament in 2022 and has very little chance of returning.Russian-speaking voters should not be treated as a single bloc with uniform behaviour, according to analyst Kits.While identity politics remain a factor, a growing share of this electorate is now driven by economic and social concerns.That shift is visible in Daugavpils, where Valentin Trofimov, a 62-year-old watch repairman, says he will vote for Slesers' party.His reasons are straightforward — the country, he says, "lacks money for everything", including transport, education and medicine. "Wages are too low," he said.
